alignments.note: Adversative δέ rendered by the clause-initial But; postpositive in Greek, fronted in English under rule 15.
Emphatic nominative pronoun realized separately from the verb's own inflection.
Aorist rendered by the English present perfect; the auxiliary have is the verb's own helper under rule 9, and rule 17 puts the head on the lexical verb rather than the auxiliary.

The article's complement is the substantival adjective `πτωχόν`, so under rule 49 nothing else can carry the determiner and the supplied nominal *man* is the article's own as well: `τὸ τρίτον` → *the third part* gives *the … part* to the article and *third* to the adjective. Rule 22 then heads the unit on the nominal word and never on the determiner, so the head is *man*. The discontinuity is licensed by rule 15. Competing reading: give the article a bare *the* and *poor man* to the adjective on rule 17's generic-noun clause (*good thing* on *good*); declined under rule 66's closing clause, which holds rules 22, 49 and 58 untouched where the supplied word answers to an article. The corpus agrees: every unit finalized since rule 49 entered the contract reads this shape the article's way — twelve to none — and JAS.1.11's `ὁ πλούσιος` → *the rich man* is the same lexeme family in the preceding chapter, its head corrected from *the* to *man*. The anarthrous `πτωχός` → *a poor man* at JAS.2.2 is the licensed contrast, no article standing there to take either word. Rule 57 does not bear on this: no genitive is interposed.

Substantival adjective, left with a bare poor because the article beside it takes both the determiner and the supplied nominal under rule 49. Rule 58's substantival-takes-the-determiner arm is not the case, an article being present.

Ordinary negative οὐ aligned to not. Rule 44 does not apply: this is a negative particle in a question expecting an affirmative answer, not an interrogative μή, and the ASV writes a word for it. The competing reading gives the do-support Do to οὐχ as well; see the note on s009.
Article realized by the under rule 19.
Substantival adjective with no supplied generic noun; the determiner is the article's under rules 19 and 58.

Do-support auxiliary and lexical verb, discontinuous under rule 15; head on the lexical verb under rule 17. The clause is a yes/no question, so English requires do-support for subject-verb inversion whether or not a negator stands in it, which makes Do the inflected verb's own auxiliary under rule 9 rather than a word answering to οὐχ. The competing reading attaches Do to the negator on the ground that English negation also forces do-support; it remains defensible, but the interrogative inversion alone would have produced it.
Genitive complement of καταδυναστεύω rendered as the plain English object you.
Coordinating conjunction realized by and; an expressed Greek conjunction, so rules 88 and 98 are not in question.
Intensive αὐτοί rendered by the emphatic reflexive themselves.
Finite verb; the interrogative Do of the coordinated first clause is not repeated here, so the verb stands alone.
Preposition realized by before; rule 36 keeps the English preposition that governs the phrase on the Greek preposition rather than reading drag before as phrasal.

Anarthrous Greek noun, so the supplied *the* is an ordinary rule 7 helper on the word it determines under rule 51's anarthrous clause, as JHN.19.13's *the judgment seat* has it, and no article competes for it. *Judgment seats* is the ASV's compound gloss of κριτήριον and no separate source token answers to either word. Rule 91's operational test decides the head and both candidate words are already spent in the corpus: the κρι- family heads on the *judgment*/*judge* word in all 67 of its units — `κρίσις` 23, `κρίμα` 8, `κρίνω` 36, none conceding — while *seat* is `βῆμα`'s own gloss at 2CO.5.10 and JHN.19.13, 2CO.5.10's note saying in terms that *seat* glosses βῆμα and *judgment* modifies it, and `θρόνος` takes *throne* in all 47 of its units. So *seats* is the supplied generic completion here and *judgment* is what realizes this lexeme, exactly as `σπουδή` → *earnest care* heads on *earnest* and `πραιτώριον` → *praetorian guard* on *praetorian* under rule 66. The competing head on *seats* is the accepted reading's, argued from κριτήριον denoting the tribunal rather than the act of judging; that is the denotational decomposition rule 99 names as the recurring failure and rule 91 replaces with a query on the lemma, and rule 66's `ζῷον` → *living creature* does not reach it, *creature* being a gloss of `ζῷον` where *seat* is another lexeme's.

review_notes: Every s### and t### id is partitioned exactly once; no unrepresented or added units were needed, and every unit is aligned.

Changed from the accepted alignment: the supplied man (t007) moves from πτωχόν to the article τόν, and the article's unit heads on man. Rule 49 states in terms that where an article's complement is an adjective, nothing else can carry the determiner and a supplied nominal is the article's own (τὸ τρίτον → the third part), and rule 22 heads such a unit on the nominal word and never on the determiner. The accepted reading cited rule 57, which does not apply here — no genitive is interposed between the article and what it governs — and rule 17's generic-noun clause, which decides the head inside a unit rather than which token owns the supplied noun. The accepted reading remains defensible and is named in the s004 note.

Unchanged but materially contested: the do-support Do (t008) stays with the finite verb s009 rather than with the negator s006. The accepted note justified this on the negation alone; the better ground is that the clause is an interrogative, so inversion requires do-support independently, which makes it the verb's own auxiliary under rule 9.

Unchanged but contested: s016 heads on seats rather than judgment. This is a rule 66/91 question that a corpus query on κριτήριον and on βῆμα would settle better than the reasoning available in the verse; the note names the competing reading and the units that support it.
A reference comparison should report the article τόν as covering the discontinuous the … man; that is the rule 49 reading and not an error.
